question: What does greedy decoding do at each step?
options: Picks the least likely token to increase diversity
explanation: Greedy decoding takes the argmax of the next-token distribution, so it is deterministic.

question: What happens to the next-token distribution when you lower the temperature below 1?
options: Tokens are removed from the vocabulary
It becomes sharper, concentrating mass on the most likely tokens
explanation: Dividing logits by T < 1 magnifies the gaps between them, so the softmax puts more mass on the top tokens.

question: Why does top-p adapt better than top-k to the model's confidence?
options: Top-p keeps a variable number of tokens: few when the distribution is peaked, many when it is flat
Top-p always keeps more tokens than top-k
Top-p does not require a softmax
explanation: Top-p keeps the smallest set reaching cumulative probability p, so its size follows the shape of the distribution; top-k always keeps exactly k.

question: With temperature 1.5 and no other filter, how many vocabulary tokens can be sampled?
options: All of them, since temperature never sets a probability to zero
explanation: Temperature rescales logits but keeps them finite, so every token keeps a nonzero probability. Only top-k or top-p truncate.

question: In the experiment, beam search produced the highest log-likelihood. Why is it still a poor default for open-ended text?
options: It is too slow to run
The most likely sequence tends to be dull, repetitive or a verbatim quote of training data
It cannot use a causal mask
explanation: High-likelihood text is not human-like text; beam search excels when there is one correct answer, such as translation.

question: Why does beam search sum log-probabilities instead of multiplying probabilities?
options: Products of many probabilities below 1 underflow to zero
explanation: Summing logs is numerically stable and ranks sequences exactly the same way as the product.
